frontmatter.title: Cognitive Evaluation Theory: How External Events Shape Intrinsic Motivation — A Focused Analysis
aliases: CET — Functional Significance and Intrinsic Motivation
frontmatter.analytical-focus: How does the functional significance of an external event — specifically whether it registers as controlling or informational — determine whether that event enhances or undermines intrinsic motivation, and what cognitive-evaluative processes mediate this relationship?

key-frameworks.name: Cognitive Evaluation Theory
key-frameworks.description: Sub-theory of SDT explaining how external events affect intrinsic motivation through their impact on perceived autonomy and perceived competence
key-frameworks.validation: High — supported by meta-analyses and cross-cultural replication

key-frameworks.name: Perceived Locus of Causality Framework
key-frameworks.description: Theoretical lens for understanding whether individuals attribute their behaviour to internal or external causes
key-frameworks.developers: de Charms (1968); refined by Deci & Ryan
key-frameworks.validation: High — theoretically central, empirically operationalised through multiple instruments

key-frameworks.name: Functional Significance Taxonomy
key-frameworks.description: Classification of ambient conditions as controlling, informational, or amotivating based on their perceived primary function
key-frameworks.validation: Medium-High — compelling theoretically, but operationalisation remains contested

frontmatter.target-audience: Instructional designers, educational psychologists, and graduate students with foundational knowledge of motivation theory and SDT
key-arguments: The same external event (e.g., a reward) can either undermine or enhance intrinsic motivation depending on its functional significance — the relative salience of its controlling versus informational aspect
Intrinsic motivation is mediated by two separable psychological needs: autonomy (PLOC) and competence, and external events affect these two pathways differentially

The undermining of intrinsic motivation by controlling events is not simply an artefact of reward structures but reflects a fundamental principle about human agency and the conditions that sustain self-directed engagement
key-distinctions: Controlling vs. informational functional significance — the most important distinction in CET
Task-contingent vs. performance-contingent vs. completion-contingent rewards — the three reward structures with meaningfully different motivational effects
Competence pathway vs. autonomy pathway — two separable mediating mechanisms explaining how external events reach motivational outcomes

expansion-topics.description: CET posits autonomy and competence as mediating mechanisms, but BPNT provides the fuller theoretical architecture for understanding psychological needs as universal nutriments for growth. An expansion here would examine how need satisfaction and need frustration differ, and what the implications are for instructional contexts.

CET focuses on the source of motivation (intrinsic vs. extrinsic); EVT focuses on the structure of motivation (expectancy × value). Comparing these two frameworks exposes important complementarities and reveals where each is inadequate alone — particularly around how task value interacts with autonomy perceptions.

CET's informational/controlling distinction maps directly onto the feedback literature, where normative feedback (controlling) and mastery-referenced feedback (informational) have markedly different effects. A focused analysis here would bridge CET with the feedback research tradition.

Gamification typically layers extrinsic reward structures onto intrinsically motivating activities — precisely the scenario CET predicts will undermine motivation. A focused analysis would examine when gamification enhances vs. undermines engagement using CET as the theoretical lens.

Applied analysis of what it actually means to create an autonomy-supportive learning environment — not just removing controlling language but actively supporting internalization through rationale provision, acknowledgment of negative affect, and reliance on non-controlling language.

Growth mindset interventions frequently involve praise strategies — but the functional significance of that praise matters enormously for whether it enhances or undermines intrinsic motivation. Examining how Dweck's work intersects with CET's praise research reveals important nuances for instructional designers.

empirical-support: Deci, Koestner & Ryan (1999) meta-analysis of 128 studies
Lepper, Greene & Nisbett (1973) — foundational overjustification experiment
limitations-noted: Operationalisation of functional significance is theoretically post-hoc in many studies
Most foundational research conducted in WEIRD populations
Meta-analytic battles expose sensitivity to coding decisions

callouts.title: Prediction Point
callouts.body: Before reading further, commit to a prediction: Suppose a child who genuinely loves drawing is given a gold-star certificate every time they complete a drawing. After several weeks, the certificates stop. Does the child draw *more*, *less*, or *about the same* as before the reward programme began? Write down your prediction and the intuition behind it. The answer — and the explanation — is the core of what this report analyses.

callouts.title: Intrinsic Motivation (Deci & Ryan, 1985)
callouts.body: Motivation that arises from the inherent interest, enjoyment, or satisfaction of an activity itself, independent of separable outcomes. An intrinsically motivated person engages in an activity because it is experienced as freely chosen, interesting, and inherently rewarding. The prototypical markers are: voluntary initiation, persistence in the absence of external prompts, positive affect during engagement, and free-choice resumption after an interruption. Intrinsic motivation is NOT the same as liking an activity — one can like (be positively valenced toward) an activity one is extrinsically motivated to perform. The critical property is the perceived source of regulation: intrinsic motivation is internally regulated; extrinsic motivation is regulated by anticipated consequences outside the activity itself.

callouts.title: Perceived Locus of Causality (PLOC) (de Charms, 1968; Deci & Ryan, 1985)
callouts.body: The subjective perception of the source of one's own behaviour — experienced as either originating within oneself (internal PLOC, "I chose to do this") or determined by external forces (external PLOC, "I am doing this because of outside pressure"). PLOC is not a binary state but a continuum, and it is phenomenological rather than objective: the same objectively constrained situation may register as internally caused for one person and externally caused for another. CET treats perceived locus of causality as the primary mediator linking external events to intrinsic motivation: events that shift PLOC toward the external pole undermine intrinsic motivation; events that preserve or strengthen an internal PLOC protect it. This is distinct from actual causality — the point is what the person *perceives*.

callouts.title: Functional Significance (Deci & Ryan, 1985)
callouts.body: The psychological meaning an event carries for the person who experiences it, specifically with respect to two possible aspects: the **controlling aspect** (the degree to which the event is experienced as pressuring the person to behave in a particular way, implying that the event is managing or directing behaviour) and the **informational aspect** (the degree to which the event is experienced as providing competence-relevant feedback, conveying information about how well one is doing relative to a standard). Every external event — reward, praise, deadline, feedback, surveillance — carries *both* aspects to some degree, but one tends to be more salient. It is this relative salience, not the objective nature of the event, that determines its motivational effect. Events whose controlling aspect is most salient shift PLOC external and undermine intrinsic motivation. Events whose informational aspect is most salient enhance intrinsic motivation by supporting perceived competence, provided PLOC remains internal.

callouts.title: Reward Contingency Types
callouts.body: The structural relationship between performance and reward. Three types matter most for CET: (1) **Task-contingent rewards** — given simply for participating in or completing the task, without reference to quality (e.g., "here is a sticker for drawing"). (2) **Completion-contingent rewards** — given for completing the task to a basic standard. (3) **Performance-contingent rewards** — given in proportion to quality of performance (e.g., "top marks get a prize"). CET predicts that task-contingent and completion-contingent rewards carry primarily a controlling functional significance and reliably undermine intrinsic motivation; performance-contingent rewards are more ambiguous because they also carry informational content about competence, though their controlling aspect typically dominates unless the framing is explicitly informational.

callouts.title: CET's Central Proposition
callouts.body: No external event has an intrinsically fixed effect on intrinsic motivation. Its effect is determined by the cognitive-evaluative interpretation that establishes its functional significance. Controlling events (those perceived primarily as pressure) undermine intrinsic motivation by externalising PLOC. Informational events (those perceived primarily as competence feedback) can enhance intrinsic motivation when they convey positive competence information and when PLOC remains internal. Amotivating events (those that convey neither agency nor competence — such as meaningless failure or arbitrary incompetence feedback) undermine both autonomy and competence perceptions, producing the deepest motivational damage.

callouts.title: Conceptual Checkpoint
callouts.body: The argument from here forward depends on the distinction between the controlling aspect and the informational aspect of an event. Before proceeding, test yourself: can you explain, in your own words, why the *same* verbal praise ("great job!") could be primarily controlling for one student and primarily informational for another? What factors would determine which meaning is more salient? If you're reaching for the definitions above rather than understanding them, consider re-reading before proceeding.

callouts.title: Integrating the Framework
callouts.body:
**Comprehension**: Why does CET require the concept of functional significance rather than simply categorising events as "rewards" or "not rewards"? What does functional significance explain that event-type alone cannot?

**Application**: Think of a time you received feedback on your work. Using the PLOC framework, how would you characterise your experience? What features of that feedback interaction shifted its significance toward controlling or informational?

**Extension**: CET assumes that perceived locus of causality and perceived competence are separable pathways. What would happen theoretically if an event simultaneously enhanced perceived competence but shifted PLOC external? Is this combination coherent within CET's framework?

callouts.title: Knowledge State — Before
callouts.body: Before engaging with the evidence, capture your current position: How confident are you that the undermining effect is real and robust? Rate your confidence 1–10. What evidence or experiences support your current view? Record this now — we will return to it after examining the evidence.

callouts.title: The Lepper, Greene & Nisbett (1973) Core Finding
callouts.body: Children in the expected-reward condition showed significantly lower free-choice engagement with drawing materials 1–2 weeks after the reward phase, compared to unexpected-reward and no-reward controls. Effect sizes were substantial (Cohen's d estimates from later meta-analyses place the effect around 0.4–0.5 for expected tangible rewards). This study established the "overjustification effect" as a concept — the idea that externally justifying behaviour you already enjoy paradoxically weakens your motivation to engage in it.

callouts.title: Deci, Koestner & Ryan (1999) — Key Findings from 128 Studies
callouts.body: (1) Expected tangible rewards reliably undermined intrinsic motivation as measured by free-choice behaviour (d ≈ −0.36) and self-reported interest (d ≈ −0.15). (2) Unexpected rewards did not undermine intrinsic motivation. (3) Verbal rewards (praise) enhanced intrinsic motivation when conveying positive competence information. (4) Engagement-contingent and completion-contingent tangible rewards showed the strongest undermining. (5) Performance-contingent tangible rewards showed an intermediate pattern, reflecting their dual controlling/informational character.

callouts.title: The Meta-Analysis Interpretation Battle
callouts.body: Cameron/Pierce (1994) and Deci/Koestner/Ryan (1999) analysed largely overlapping sets of studies and reached opposite conclusions. How? The disagreement is not primarily about the data — it is about *how to code the variables*. The two teams classified studies into contingency categories differently, defined "undermining" using different measurement criteria, and made different modelling choices about moderator variables. This reveals a methodological problem that is partly irresolvable: the functional significance construct is difficult to operationalise objectively. When an experiment labels a condition "expected reward," it is not obvious whether participants experienced this as primarily controlling or informational — and the researchers' coding decisions implicitly embed theoretical commitments. The dispute is not just empirical; it is partly about what counts as a fair test of the theory.

callouts.title: What the Pattern of Findings Actually Shows
callouts.body: The undermining effect is real but not universal. Expected tangible rewards for task engagement (where reward receipt does not depend on quality) reliably undermine free-choice behaviour in laboratory paradigms. This effect is medium-sized and has been replicated across decades. However, the effect is highly conditional: it does not apply to unexpected rewards, it is weakened or reversed when rewards carry genuine positive competence information, it is sensitive to whether the controlling aspect is made salient by the administration context (how the reward is presented, by whom, and in what relational context), and it is moderated by individual differences in need for autonomy. The effect is NOT a universal property of rewards-as-objects; it is a property of the psychological meaning that particular reward interactions create in specific people in specific contexts.

callouts.title: The Praise Finding Is Particularly Informative
callouts.body: Verbal rewards (praise) consistently emerge from the meta-analytic literature as enhancing rather than undermining intrinsic motivation — which is exactly what CET predicts. Praise is, structurally, a controlling event: someone in authority is evaluating you and finding you sufficient. But when praise is framed as conveying genuine competence information ("You did that correctly; you have real skill here"), it activates the informational pathway more than the controlling pathway, and the result is enhanced intrinsic motivation. This finding is important because it shows that CET's mechanism works in both directions: it is not that external events are inherently undermining; it is that the functional significance framework correctly predicts *which* events undermine and *which* enhance.

callouts.title: Prediction Check
callouts.body: Return to the prediction you made at the start of this report about the child who loves drawing. After reading the evidence, how does your prediction compare to what the research shows? If you predicted correctly, examine the reasoning behind your prediction — was it based on the CET mechanism, or did you arrive at the right answer by different logic? If you were surprised, identify which assumption was incorrect.

callouts.title: Integrating the Evidence
callouts.body:
**Comprehension**: What is the single most important finding from the evidence base for understanding CET's central claim? Why does this finding matter more than the others?

**Application**: If you were designing a study to test whether Cameron/Pierce or Deci/Koestner/Ryan are correct about performance-contingent rewards, what methodological choice would you make to resolve the ambiguity, and why?

**Extension**: Where in this evidence base do you find yourself most uncertain or resistant? Resistance is often productive — it frequently signals an assumption that is worth examining explicitly.

callouts.title: Complexity Transition
callouts.body: The analysis ahead goes beneath the evidence to examine *why* functional significance produces these effects — the causal architecture of the undermining process. This phase builds directly on the conceptual framework from Phase II and the empirical pattern from Phase III. If the distinction between controlling and informational functional significance feels clear, proceed. If it remains fuzzy, a brief return to the definitions in Phase II will strengthen what follows.

callouts.title: The Invisible Transformation of Meaning
callouts.body: What the autonomy pathway mechanism reveals is that rewards do not merely add a new reason to perform an activity alongside the pre-existing intrinsic reason. They can transform the *experienced meaning* of the activity itself. Before the reward, drawing was an act of self-expression. After repeated reward administration, drawing is an act of earning. The activity's identity — what it *is* for the person — has changed. This is why the effect persists after rewards are removed: you cannot simply subtract the reward and expect to return to the previous motivational state, because the activity's meaning has been reorganised. This is a far more radical claim than merely saying "people become accustomed to rewards" — it is a claim about how reward structures reshape the self-world relationship.

callouts.title: The Asymmetry Between Enhancement and Damage
callouts.body: The two-pathway architecture produces an interesting asymmetry: enhancing intrinsic motivation requires satisfying *both* the autonomy and competence needs simultaneously — an event must convey positive competence information *and* do so in a way that preserves internal PLOC. This is a conjunction requirement. Undermining intrinsic motivation, by contrast, requires only one pathway — either externalising PLOC *or* frustrating perceived competence will damage intrinsic motivation. This means that intrinsic motivation is harder to build than to erode. It is robust against threats from a single pathway, but only when the other pathway is actively supported. In instructional contexts, this implies that well-intentioned informational praise can be partially neutralized if delivered in a surveillance-heavy, controlling evaluative atmosphere — the competence benefit is offset by autonomy cost.

callouts.title: CET and Communicative Pragmatics: The Same Sentence, Different Speech Acts
callouts.body: Cognitive Evaluation Theory's central insight — that the same event carries different meaning depending on its functional significance — has a precise structural parallel in linguistic pragmatics, specifically [[speech act theory]] (Austin, 1962; Searle, 1969). In speech act theory, an utterance's meaning is not exhausted by its propositional content (what it literally says); its force depends on the social act it performs (a promise, a threat, a directive, an assessment). "You're good at this" can be a genuine expression of admiration (informational), a manipulative tool to elicit compliance ("since you're so good at this, you should keep doing it" — controlling), or a performance of social role. The *same surface form* carries radically different illocutionary force depending on context, relationship, power dynamics, and history. CET's functional significance is, in essence, the motivational analogue of illocutionary force: it is not what the event literally delivers but what social-psychological act it performs in the relationship that matters. This parallel suggests that CET would benefit from closer engagement with sociolinguistic and relational accounts of how competence and control signals are communicated — and why the same reward, administered by different people in different relational contexts, has such different effects.

callouts.title: The Operationalisation Problem: When Functional Significance Becomes Unfalsifiable
callouts.body: CET's most significant theoretical vulnerability is related to its greatest strength. The concept of functional significance is powerful precisely because it does not tie motivational effects to the structural properties of events — it allows the same event to have different effects depending on how it is experienced. But this flexibility comes at a cost: functional significance is extraordinarily difficult to operationalise independently of the motivational outcomes it is supposed to predict. In most studies, the researcher manipulates the event (reward type, feedback framing) and then measures intrinsic motivation. The functional significance is inferred from the outcome, not measured directly. This creates the risk of circular explanation: "The reward undermined intrinsic motivation because it was controlling; how do we know it was controlling? Because it undermined intrinsic motivation." The studies that get closest to independent measurement of functional significance (using manipulation checks, thought-listing procedures, or phenomenological reports) provide more compelling evidence — but they remain the minority. This is not a fatal flaw but a persistent limitation that needs to be held in mind when interpreting the evidence base.

callouts.title: Calibration Check
callouts.body: Rate your current understanding of the two-pathway model on a scale of 1–10. Now, without looking back, explain: under what specific conditions would you predict that a performance-contingent reward would *enhance* intrinsic motivation rather than undermine it? What conditions would need to be satisfied simultaneously? If you cannot specify the conditions clearly, re-reading the autonomy/competence pathway sections will sharpen your model.

callouts.title: Integrating the Mechanisms
callouts.body:
**Comprehension**: What is the functional difference between the autonomy pathway and the competence pathway in CET? Can you think of a real-world scenario in which an external event would harm intrinsic motivation through the autonomy pathway but protect it through the competence pathway — and what would the net effect likely be?

**Application**: Consider a gamified learning system that awards badges for completing tasks regardless of performance quality. Using the two-pathway model, trace the predicted motivational effects. What specific features of the badge system determine whether the autonomy or competence pathway is more activated?

**Extension**: The temporal dynamics section suggests that the undermining effect builds gradually with repeated reward exposure. What would a theory of motivational recovery look like? If rewards erode intrinsic motivation over time, is there a corresponding process by which intrinsic motivation can be restored — and what would drive it?

callouts.title: Designing Informational Rather Than Controlling Feedback
callouts.body: Effective feedback under CET principles: (1) References the person's own prior performance rather than comparative norms — progress feedback is more informational, rank feedback is more controlling. (2) Uses language that attributes performance to internal competencies ("you found an efficient approach") rather than external compliance ("you followed the instructions correctly"). (3) Is delivered in a context where the relationship is characterised by autonomy support — acknowledgment of the person's perspective, explanations rather than directives, non-controlling language. (4) Avoids surveillance-like monitoring that makes the evaluative relationship salient even in the absence of explicit evaluative events.

callouts.title: The Gamification Paradox
callouts.body: The activities most commonly targeted for gamification are those that educators and designers perceive as insufficiently engaging — and the addition of game mechanics is intended to supply the missing motivation. But CET predicts that if the activity was already somewhat intrinsically interesting (or had the potential to become so with appropriate autonomy-supportive framing), the addition of controlling reward structures will damage that potential. Gamification often imports the motivational dynamics of extrinsic contingency precisely where intrinsic motivation was most valuable to preserve. The question to ask before gamifying is not "will this increase engagement?" (it often will, in the short term) but "what kind of engagement, through what motivational mechanism, and at what cost to intrinsic interest?"

callouts.title: Knowledge State — After
callouts.body: Return to what you recorded at the start of Phase III. How has your position changed? Specifically: did the evidence shift your view on the robustness of the undermining effect? On the conditions under which it operates? On the practical implications? The distinction between additive learning (adding information to a stable framework) and structural learning (reorganising the framework itself) is diagnostic of depth of engagement with the material.

callouts.title: Integrating the Implications
callouts.body:
**Comprehension**: What is the most important limitation of CET for a practitioner who wants to apply it to a specific educational context? How should that limitation change what the practitioner does?

**Application**: You are designing a formative assessment strategy for a secondary school science class. Using CET principles, what three design decisions would you make, and why?

**Extension**: CET focuses on how external events affect *existing* intrinsic motivation. But what about situations where the learner has no intrinsic motivation at the start — where the content is perceived as boring or irrelevant? Does CET say anything useful about how to cultivate intrinsic motivation from a low base, or is it essentially a theory about protecting something that already exists?

callouts.title: The Interpretive Filter Model of Functional Significance
callouts.body:
Synthesising CET's core architecture with the evidence on moderating factors and the temporal dynamics section, I propose a model that makes the functional significance concept more tractable for both research and practice. Rather than treating functional significance as a property of events (or even of events-in-context), the model treats it as the output of an *interpretive filter* — a relatively stable, individual-level attentional and evaluative orientation that determines which aspects of external events are most salient for a given person at a given time.

The interpretive filter has three components:

**(1) The relational frame**: The established meaning-structure of the evaluative relationship between the person and the source of the external event (teacher, employer, parent, system). This frame is built up through history and cannot be altered by a single event; it acts as a background context within which new events are interpreted. A controlling relational frame means that even genuinely informational events will be partly assimilated to a controlling interpretation; an autonomy-supportive relational frame allows informational events to be received as such.

**(2) The motivational history with the specific activity**: Whether the activity has previously been predominantly internally or externally regulated. Activities with a long history of intrinsic engagement have a "motivational baseline" that is more resistant to controlling events; activities with a history of extrinsic regulation are more vulnerable to further externalisation of PLOC because the internal referent for the activity's value has already been weakened.

**(3) The dispositional orientation**: The individual's relatively stable tendency to orient toward internal versus external causality (captured in SDT by Causality Orientations Theory). Autonomy-oriented individuals maintain internal PLOC more readily under controlling conditions; control-oriented individuals are more vulnerable to the undermining effect.

What this model adds to standard CET is a mechanism for understanding why the *same* event produces such different effects across people and contexts: the interpretive filter is doing real work, not as a passive receiver but as an active constructor of meaning. It also provides a leverage point for intervention: rather than focusing only on event properties (making rewards informational), practitioners should attend to the relational frame (building an autonomy-supportive relationship context over time) and the motivational history (avoiding early externalisation of regulation for activities where intrinsic interest is the goal). The event-level and relationship-level interventions are not substitutes; they operate at different timescales and through different mechanisms.

callouts.title: Motivational Asymmetry and Instructional Design Sequencing
callouts.body: The temporal asymmetry between undermining (fast-acting, hard to reverse) and enhancement (slow-building, fragile) has direct implications for the *sequencing* of external events in instructional contexts. Specifically: the damage done by early controlling events in a learning sequence is disproportionately costly relative to late controlling events, because early events shape the interpretive filter through which subsequent events are processed. A teacher who begins the year with high-stakes, controlling evaluation practices, then shifts to autonomy-supportive practices mid-year, will likely achieve lower intrinsic motivation outcomes than a teacher who maintains autonomy-supportive practices throughout — even if the total "dose" of controlling events is identical. The order matters. This is not explicitly stated in standard CET, but it follows directly from the interaction between temporal dynamics and the interpretive filter model. Instructional designers should treat the first exposures to a domain or activity as particularly high-stakes for motivational architecture, not merely for knowledge structure.

callouts.title: Final Integration
callouts.body:
**Comprehension**: What is the single insight from this entire analysis that most changes how you think about the relationship between external conditions and intrinsic motivation? Can you state it in one sentence?

**Application**: Explain the essence of CET and its most practically important implication in three sentences to a colleague who has not read this report.

**Extension**: The Interpretive Filter Model proposes that the relational frame and motivational history mediate how events are interpreted. What would a research programme designed to test this model look like, and what would constitute strong evidence for or against it?

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Internal PKB Connections:**

- **[[Self-Determination Theory]]** — CET is architecturally nested within SDT as one of its six mini-theories. The SDT Foundational Report establishes the framework (basic psychological needs, the self-determination continuum, the three needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness) within which CET operates. This focused analysis deepens the SDT treatment by examining precisely how autonomy and competence needs are affected by specific external events — a mechanism the Foundational Report gestures toward but does not fully unpack. The two documents are best read as complementary layers: SDT provides the map; CET provides the geological core sample through the motivation mechanism layer.

- **[[Self-Regulated Learning]]** — The SRL report examines how learners regulate their cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational processes. CET connects to SRL through the motivational regulation dimension: the degree to which a learner is intrinsically versus extrinsically regulated determines their regulatory strategy selection, persistence, and deep processing engagement. Learners with internally regulated motivation engage in more effective self-regulatory processes. Conversely, external reward structures that undermine intrinsic motivation (per CET) would be expected to simultaneously degrade self-regulatory quality — particularly the autonomous goal-setting and self-evaluation processes that SRL depends on. The CET → SRL pathway is undertheorised in the literature and represents a promising integration target.

- **[[Cognitive Load Theory]]** — CLT and CET address different aspects of the learning situation (cognitive architecture vs. motivational architecture), but they intersect in important ways. High extrinsic motivation under controlling conditions may produce surface processing (focused on completing the task to obtain the reward) that aligns with lower cognitive investment — potentially increasing extraneous cognitive load while reducing germane load. Conversely, high intrinsic motivation, by producing deeper engagement with the material's structure, may facilitate the kind of elaborative processing that builds schemas (the goal of CLT-informed instruction). This is a connection neither theory makes explicit, but exploring it would deepen understanding of why motivationally-optimal conditions tend also to be cognitively-optimal conditions.

- **[[Attribution Theory]]** — Weiner's attribution theory addresses how people explain their successes and failures. CET's PLOC construct is conceptually related to Weiner's locus of control dimension, but they are not identical: PLOC in CET is specifically about the perceived cause of *behaviour* (internal vs. external), while locus of control in attribution theory is about the perceived cause of *outcomes* (success/failure). The intersection is particularly important for understanding how competence feedback interacts with attributional patterns: negative feedback attributed to controllable, internal causes (effort) has different motivational effects than the same feedback attributed to stable, internal causes (lack of ability) — and CET's competence pathway prediction depends on this attributional dimension without fully theorising it.

**Cross-Report Links:**

- **[[Self-Determination Theory — Foundational Report]]** — This focused analysis extends the foundational SDT treatment by providing a detailed mechanistic account of how external conditions affect the intrinsic/extrinsic motivation dimension. It adds the functional significance concept, the two-pathway model, and the temporal asymmetry analysis as layers that the Foundational Report does not cover in depth. Together, the two documents constitute a comprehensive treatment of SDT's motivation architecture.

**Synthetic Observation**: CET occupies a distinctive position in the PKB — it provides the most fine-grained motivational mechanism account currently available, but it connects outward to both the macro-level motivational architecture of SDT and the micro-level cognitive architecture of CLT and SRL. It is a bridge theory, and its greatest analytical value comes from examining it in relationship to these adjacent frameworks rather than in isolation. The knowledge network emerging across the SRL, CLT, and SDT reports suggests a coherent underlying theme: effective learning requires conditions that simultaneously optimise cognitive processing, motivational quality, and regulatory engagement — and these three dimensions are deeply interdependent rather than separable.

callouts.title: Amotivation
callouts.body: A state in which the person lacks any sense of agency with respect to an activity — neither intrinsic motivation (engagement for its own sake) nor extrinsic motivation (engagement for separable outcomes). Amotivation is the motivational consequence of events that simultaneously frustrate perceived competence and externalise PLOC to the point of helplessness. It is the deepest form of motivational damage in the SDT framework and is associated with disengagement, helplessness, and eventually dropout. Amotivation is distinct from low intrinsic motivation — one can be extrinsically motivated (working for rewards) without being amotivated.

callouts.title: Autonomy Orientation (from Causality Orientations Theory)
callouts.body: An individual-level difference variable describing the general tendency to orient toward the autonomous aspects of environments — to notice and be regulated by features that support interest, value, and personal meaning. Autonomy-oriented individuals show attenuated undermining effects in response to controlling events. They are not *immune* to functional significance effects, but their interpretive filter has a stronger default bias toward internal PLOC. Contrasts with *control orientation* (tendency to be regulated by controlling features) and *impersonal orientation* (tendency to attribute regulation to uncontrollable forces, associated with amotivation).

callouts.title: Causality Orientations Theory (COT)
callouts.body: A mini-theory within SDT that describes individual differences in people's tendencies to orient toward particular types of motivational regulation. Not to be confused with [[attribution theory]]. COT predicts that autonomy-oriented individuals will respond differently to controlling events than control-oriented individuals, and this moderates the functional significance mechanism in CET. An important implication: identical instructional interventions will produce different motivational outcomes for individuals with different causality orientations.

callouts.title: Ego Involvement
callouts.body: A motivational state in which self-worth is contingent on performance outcomes — performance becomes a test of the person's value or adequacy rather than an expression of their interests. Ego involvement is theoretically related to the controlling pathway in CET: events that create ego involvement (typically comparative evaluation, normative feedback, and high-stakes assessment) introduce a self-esteem regulation layer that makes the activity extrinsically salient and shifts PLOC external. Harackiewicz and Manderlink (1984) showed that ego-involving praise ("you're much better than average") undermine intrinsic motivation while task-involving praise ("you've really mastered the strategy") does not.

callouts.title: Engagement-Contingent Reward
callouts.body: A reward contingent simply on engaging in or starting an activity, without reference to completion or quality. This is the most purely controlling reward type in CET's taxonomy: the contingency "if you do it, you get the reward" makes the external reason for the behaviour maximally salient. Empirically, engagement-contingent and task-contingent rewards show the strongest undermining effects in the Deci/Koestner/Ryan (1999) meta-analysis.

callouts.title: Free-Choice Behaviour
callouts.body: The dependent variable most commonly used in CET research to measure intrinsic motivation: the amount of time a person voluntarily spends with an activity when they are not required to do so, typically measured during a period when the experimenter is absent and no external contingencies are operating. Free-choice behaviour is considered a more direct behavioural measure of intrinsic motivation than self-reported interest, because it does not depend on verbal self-report. However, it also has limitations: it may reflect habit or accessibility rather than intrinsic motivation, and it is difficult to measure in ecological (non-laboratory) contexts.

callouts.title: Informational Feedback
callouts.body: Feedback whose primary functional significance is informational — it conveys genuine competence-relevant information to the recipient in a context where PLOC remains internal. Informational feedback is characterised by specificity (pointing to particular aspects of performance), mastery-referencing (comparing performance to personal standards or task standards rather than to other people), process orientation (attributing performance to strategies and effort rather than global ability), and non-controlling language (describing rather than evaluating). CET predicts that informational feedback enhances intrinsic motivation by satisfying the competence need without threatening the autonomy need.

callouts.title: Internalisation
callouts.body: The process by which externally regulated behaviours are gradually taken in and re-regulated by the self — moving along the self-determination continuum from external regulation toward identified regulation and ultimately integrated regulation. While CET specifically addresses intrinsic motivation (the far end of the intrinsic pole), Organismic Integration Theory (another SDT sub-theory) addresses internalisation of extrinsic motivation. The two processes are related: creating conditions that support autonomy and competence facilitates both intrinsic motivation (when activities are inherently interesting) and internalisation (when activities are not inherently interesting but have personal or social value).

callouts.title: Overjustification Effect
callouts.body: The specific psychological phenomenon in which adding an external justification (reward) to a behaviour that is already intrinsically motivated reduces the person's subsequent intrinsic interest in that behaviour. The term "overjustification" refers to the idea that the external reason provides more justification than is needed — and in the process, changes the person's interpretation of why they were performing the activity in the first place. Originally named by Lepper, Greene, and Nisbett (1973); theoretically explained by CET's PLOC mechanism.

callouts.title: Perceived Competence
callouts.body: The subjective sense of effectiveness in one's interactions with the environment — feeling capable, skilled, and able to produce intended outcomes. Distinct from objective competence: a person can be highly competent but have low perceived competence (as in the Impostor Phenomenon), or low competence but high perceived competence (overconfidence). In CET, perceived competence is a basic psychological need whose satisfaction by external events (through positive informational feedback) can enhance intrinsic motivation, and whose frustration (through negative feedback or task failure without informational framing) undermines intrinsic motivation.

callouts.title: Surveillance
callouts.body: The awareness of being observed or monitored, even in the absence of explicit evaluative events. CET research (Lepper & Greene, 1975) shows that surveillance carries a controlling functional significance on its own: being watched introduces an external audience, makes the evaluative relationship salient, and tends to shift PLOC external. This finding has significant implications for digital learning environments in which learner behaviour is continuously logged and monitored, even if that monitoring is not connected to explicit rewards or consequences.

callouts.title: Deci, E. L. (1971). Effects of externally mediated rewards on intrinsic motivation. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 18(1), 105–115.
callouts.body: The foundational experimental study establishing the undermining effect with monetary rewards and Soma puzzle performance. While methodologically modest by contemporary standards, this study launched a 50-year research programme. Its value for this report is as the original empirical instantiation of the claim that extrinsic rewards can reduce subsequent free-choice engagement with intrinsically interesting activities.

callouts.title: Lepper, M. R., Greene, D., & Nisbett, R. E. (1973). Undermining children's intrinsic interest with extrinsic reward: A test of the "overjustification" hypothesis. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 28(1), 129–137.
callouts.body: The paradigmatic overjustification study with preschool children and drawing materials. Methodologically important because it used a naturalistic observation measure (classroom free play) rather than laboratory free choice, providing greater ecological validity. The unexpected-reward control condition is particularly important for CET's theoretical interpretation.

callouts.title: Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (1985). *Intrinsic motivation and self-determination in human behavior*. Plenum.
callouts.body: The theoretical monograph that articulates Cognitive Evaluation Theory as a formal sub-theory and situates it within SDT. The most important primary source for understanding CET's conceptual architecture, including the functional significance concept, the two-pathway model, and the taxonomy of ambient conditions. Essential reading for anyone working seriously with CET.

callouts.title: Cameron, J., & Pierce, W. D. (1994). Reinforcement, reward, and intrinsic motivation: A meta-analysis. *Review of Educational Research*, 64(3), 363–423.
callouts.body: The controversial meta-analysis arguing that rewards do not reliably undermine intrinsic motivation. Important as a cautionary methodological counterweight to uncritical acceptance of CET's claims. This report treats Cameron and Pierce's work not as refuting CET but as demonstrating the sensitivity of meta-analytic conclusions to coding and modelling decisions — and as providing useful disaggregation of reward types.

callouts.title: Deci, E. L., Koestner, R., & Ryan, R. M. (1999). A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation. *Psychological Bulletin*, 125(6), 627–668.
callouts.body: The comprehensive meta-analysis of 128 studies that provides the strongest evidence base for CET. The disaggregated findings by reward contingency type (engagement-contingent, completion-contingent, performance-contingent, verbal) are particularly important for instructional design applications. The exchange with Cameron and Pierce in the same issue of Psychological Bulletin is essential reading for understanding the limits of meta-analytic evidence.

callouts.title: Lepper, M. R., & Greene, D. (1975). Turning play into work: Effects of adult surveillance and extrinsic rewards on children's intrinsic motivation. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 31(3), 479–486.
callouts.body: The surveillance study showing that adult observation alone — without rewards or explicit evaluation — reduces intrinsic motivation. Important for this report because it demonstrates that the controlling functional significance can be activated without any formal reward structure, with implications for the design of digital learning environments and monitoring systems.

callouts.title: Harackiewicz, J. M., & Manderlink, G. (1984). A process analysis of the effects of performance-contingent rewards on intrinsic motivation. *Journal of Experimental Social Psychology*, 20(6), 531–551.
callouts.body: Distinguishes between ego-involving and task-involving performance feedback in the context of performance-contingent rewards. Shows that the same performance-contingent reward can either undermine (when delivered with ego-involving framing) or protect (when delivered with task-involving, informational framing) intrinsic motivation. Critical for understanding why the meta-analytic effects for performance-contingent rewards are smaller and more variable than for task-contingent rewards.

callouts.title: Ryan, R. M., Mims, V., & Koestner, R. (1983). Relation of reward contingency and interpersonal context to intrinsic motivation: A review and test using cognitive evaluation theory. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 45(4), 736–750.
callouts.body: Examines the interaction between reward contingency and the relational context in which rewards are administered. Demonstrates that performance-contingent rewards can enhance intrinsic motivation when administered in an autonomy-supportive interpersonal context and with explicitly informational language — providing important nuance for instructional applications.

callouts.title: Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (2000). The "what" and "why" of goal pursuits: Human needs and the self-determination of behavior. *Psychological Inquiry*, 11(4), 227–268.
callouts.body: Comprehensive theoretical synthesis of SDT including CET, situating the theory within broader human motivation research and responding to critics. Particularly useful for understanding how CET connects to the other SDT mini-theories (Basic Psychological Needs Theory, Causality Orientations Theory, Organismic Integration Theory) and for understanding the empirical status of the basic needs postulate.

callouts.title: Vansteenkiste, M., Lens, W., & Deci, E. L. (2006). Intrinsic versus extrinsic goal contents in self-determination theory: Another look at the quality of academic motivation. *Educational Psychologist*, 41(1), 19–31.
callouts.body: Extends CET into the educational domain, examining how intrinsic versus extrinsic goal framing (not just reward structures) affects the quality of motivation and learning outcomes. Shows that learning activities framed around intrinsic goals (curiosity, mastery, personal relevance) produce better outcomes than the same activities framed around extrinsic goals (grades, approval, performance) — consistent with CET's functional significance mechanism.

callouts.title: Austin, J. L. (1962). *How to Do Things with Words*. Oxford University Press.
callouts.body: The foundational text for speech act theory. Included in this report's reference list because of the analytical connection drawn in Phase IV between CET's functional significance concept and Austin's distinction between locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts. Specifically: the idea that an utterance's meaning is not in its propositional content but in the social act it performs maps precisely onto CET's claim that an external event's motivational effect is not in its structural properties but in the psychological function it performs.

callouts.title: Research Grounding for This Report
callouts.body:
This report draws on the experimental and meta-analytic literature on Cognitive Evaluation Theory, the primary theoretical sources (Deci & Ryan, 1971–2000), and the meta-analytic debates (Cameron & Pierce, 1994; Deci, Koestner & Ryan, 1999). The claims in Phases III and IV are grounded in well-replicated empirical findings, though the specific effect sizes cited are drawn from meta-analytic estimates and should be treated as approximations. The functional significance mechanism is theoretically well-established within SDT, though the operationalisation problem identified in Phase IV represents a genuine empirical limitation.

The analytical contributions in Phases IV and VI — specifically the claim about the asymmetry between undermining and enhancement, the cross-domain connection to speech act theory, and the Interpretive Filter Model — are original syntheses by Claude that go beyond what individual sources establish. They are grounded in the evidence and logic presented throughout the report, but they should be treated as theoretical proposals rather than established findings. The Interpretive Filter Model in particular is a novel integration that has not been formally tested; it is offered as a framework that makes the functional significance concept more tractable, not as an empirically confirmed account.

callouts.title: Deepening Your Analysis
callouts.body:
> [!topic-idea] [[Basic Psychological Needs Theory]]
> CET is one of six SDT mini-theories, and it posits autonomy and competence as mediating mechanisms without fully developing their status as universal psychological needs. Basic Psychological Needs Theory (BPNT) provides this foundational layer, arguing that autonomy, competence, and relatedness are three universal organismic needs whose satisfaction predicts well-being and whose frustration predicts ill-being — across cultures, activities, and developmental stages. A focused analysis of BPNT would deepen the CET account by examining the need satisfaction/frustration asymmetry more carefully, connecting to the hedonic and eudaimonic well-being literature, and addressing the cross-cultural evidence that is both supportive and challenging for the universality claim.

> [!topic-idea] [[Feedback Effects on Motivation and Learning]]
> CET's distinction between informational and controlling events maps most directly onto the feedback literature in educational psychology. A focused analysis here would synthesise CET with the Kluger and DeNisi (1996) meta-analysis of feedback effects, Hattie's feedback research, Shute's formative feedback framework, and the growing literature on computer-delivered feedback. The specific question is: what features of feedback operationalise CET's informational vs. controlling distinction in ways that are testable in educational contexts, and how does feedback design interact with the relational frame and motivational history constructs from the Interpretive Filter Model?

> [!topic-idea] [[Expectancy-Value Theory]]
> EVT (Eccles, Wigfield) and CET approach motivation from different directions: EVT focuses on the cognitive appraisal of tasks (do I expect to succeed? does this task have value for me?), while CET focuses on the source of regulation (am I doing this for internal or external reasons?). These frameworks are frequently treated as competitors, but they are better understood as complementary: EVT explains the structure of motivation (what determines whether someone will engage), while CET explains the quality and sustainability of motivation (what determines whether engagement is internally vs. externally regulated). A focused comparative analysis would map the intersection points, identify where each is insufficient alone, and propose an integration.

> [!topic-idea] [[Growth Mindset and CET]]
> Dweck's growth vs. fixed mindset framework shares important territory with CET — particularly around praise, competence feedback, and the effects of evaluative contexts on motivation and persistence. But the two frameworks make somewhat different predictions and are grounded in different theoretical mechanisms (implicit theories of ability vs. functional significance of feedback). A focused analysis would compare their predictions for specific instructional scenarios, examine where they converge (process praise) and diverge (the role of challenge and difficulty), and ask what an integrated account would look like.

> [!topic-idea] [[Gamification in Educational Contexts]]
> Gamification is the application of game-design elements (points, badges, leaderboards, progress bars, challenges) to non-game contexts, typically with the goal of increasing engagement. CET predicts that many common gamification elements introduce controlling functional significance and will undermine intrinsic motivation in the medium-to-long term, even if they increase short-term engagement. But the picture is more complicated: some game elements (challenge structures, mastery feedback, narrative framing) may activate the informational pathway. A focused analysis would use CET as a primary theoretical lens to evaluate specific gamification elements, develop a CET-informed gamification design framework, and examine the emerging empirical literature on gamification outcomes.

The mechanism here operates at the level of psychological freedom. [[Self-determination]] is not just a philosophical value; within SDT, it is a basic psychological need whose satisfaction is necessary for well-being and sustained motivation. When PLOC shifts external, that need is frustrated. The activity may continue — extrinsic motivation can maintain behaviour for extended periods — but the phenomenological quality of engagement changes. Intrinsic motivation, which requires that the activity be experienced as volitional, diminishes.

wiki_links.section: The Temporal Dynamics of Functional Significance
wiki_links.context_line: > Cognitive Evaluation Theory's central insight — that the same event carries different meaning depending on its functional significance — has a precise structural parallel in linguistic pragmatics, specifically [[speech act theory]] (Austin, 1962; Searle, 1969). In speech act theory, an utterance's meaning is not exhausted by its propositional content (what it literally says); its force depends on the social act it performs (a promise, a threat, a directive, an assessment). "You're good at this" can be a genuine expression of admiration (informational), a manipulative tool to elicit compliance ("since you're so good at this, you should keep doing it" — controlling), or a performance of social role. The *same surface form* carries radically different illocutionary force depending on context, relationship, power dynamics, and history. CET's functional significance is, in essence, the motivational analogue of illocutionary force: it is not what the event literally delivers but what social-psychological act it performs in the relationship that matters. This parallel suggests that CET would benefit from closer engagement with sociolinguistic and relational accounts of how competence and control signals are communicated — and why the same reward, administered by different people in different relational contexts, has such different effects.

**Game-based learning and gamification**: [[Gamification]] in educational contexts — adding point systems, badges, leaderboards, and achievement structures to learning activities — is, from a CET perspective, a practice that systematically layers controlling functional significance onto activities. This does not mean gamification always undermines intrinsic motivation, but it means the burden of proof should be on demonstrating that the specific game elements preserve rather than damage the informational significance of engagement. Leaderboards, in particular, are highly problematic: they make social comparison salient, activate external reference frames for competence evaluation, and convert intrinsically satisfying performance into ranked instrumentality.

**Individual differences are underspecified**: CET predicts that controlling events undermine intrinsic motivation on average, but individuals differ substantially in how sensitive they are to this effect. People with high [[autonomy orientation]] (from SDT's [[Causality Orientations Theory]]) show smaller undermining effects; people with high [[control orientation]] may actually show facilitated performance under controlling conditions, at least in the short term. CET's current theoretical architecture does not fully integrate these individual difference moderators — it acknowledges them, but they are not part of the core explanatory model.

wiki_links.section: Phase VII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Self-Determination Theory]]** — CET is architecturally nested within SDT as one of its six mini-theories. The SDT Foundational Report establishes the framework (basic psychological needs, the self-determination continuum, the three needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness) within which CET operates. This focused analysis deepens the SDT treatment by examining precisely how autonomy and competence needs are affected by specific external events — a mechanism the Foundational Report gestures toward but does not fully unpack. The two documents are best read as complementary layers: SDT provides the map; CET provides the geological core sample through the motivation mechanism layer.

wiki_links.section: Phase VII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Self-Regulated Learning]]** — The SRL report examines how learners regulate their cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational processes. CET connects to SRL through the motivational regulation dimension: the degree to which a learner is intrinsically versus extrinsically regulated determines their regulatory strategy selection, persistence, and deep processing engagement. Learners with internally regulated motivation engage in more effective self-regulatory processes. Conversely, external reward structures that undermine intrinsic motivation (per CET) would be expected to simultaneously degrade self-regulatory quality — particularly the autonomous goal-setting and self-evaluation processes that SRL depends on. The CET → SRL pathway is undertheorised in the literature and represents a promising integration target.

wiki_links.section: Phase VII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Cognitive Load Theory]]** — CLT and CET address different aspects of the learning situation (cognitive architecture vs. motivational architecture), but they intersect in important ways. High extrinsic motivation under controlling conditions may produce surface processing (focused on completing the task to obtain the reward) that aligns with lower cognitive investment — potentially increasing extraneous cognitive load while reducing germane load. Conversely, high intrinsic motivation, by producing deeper engagement with the material's structure, may facilitate the kind of elaborative processing that builds schemas (the goal of CLT-informed instruction). This is a connection neither theory makes explicit, but exploring it would deepen understanding of why motivationally-optimal conditions tend also to be cognitively-optimal conditions.

wiki_links.section: Phase VII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Attribution Theory]]** — Weiner's attribution theory addresses how people explain their successes and failures. CET's PLOC construct is conceptually related to Weiner's locus of control dimension, but they are not identical: PLOC in CET is specifically about the perceived cause of *behaviour* (internal vs. external), while locus of control in attribution theory is about the perceived cause of *outcomes* (success/failure). The intersection is particularly important for understanding how competence feedback interacts with attributional patterns: negative feedback attributed to controllable, internal causes (effort) has different motivational effects than the same feedback attributed to stable, internal causes (lack of ability) — and CET's competence pathway prediction depends on this attributional dimension without fully theorising it.

wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Self-Determination Theory — Foundational Report]]** — This focused analysis extends the foundational SDT treatment by providing a detailed mechanistic account of how external conditions affect the intrinsic/extrinsic motivation dimension. It adds the functional significance concept, the two-pathway model, and the temporal asymmetry analysis as layers that the Foundational Report does not cover in depth. Together, the two documents constitute a comprehensive treatment of SDT's motivation architecture.

> A mini-theory within SDT that describes individual differences in people's tendencies to orient toward particular types of motivational regulation. Not to be confused with [[attribution theory]]. COT predicts that autonomy-oriented individuals will respond differently to controlling events than control-oriented individuals, and this moderates the functional significance mechanism in CET. An important implication: identical instructional interventions will produce different motivational outcomes for individuals with different causality orientations.
